solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: It caters for visits re octane (7,7)

definitions.text: It caters for visits re octane

indicators.note: To cater is an old word for setting something askew, diagonally, so the letters are moved about.

annotation.surface: A description of a place that looks after people calling in about fuel.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the definition and the wordplay. "Caters" reads as providing for customers, but in its rare sense of setting askew it tells you to rearrange the letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A service station is where motorists stop to fill up with fuel, octane being the measure of petrol quality.

clue.text: Not all there is can deter brat being troublesome (14)

indicators.note: Something troublesome is unruly, so the letters are out of order.

annotation.surface: Someone half-listening wonders whether a bad-tempered child can be put off misbehaving.
annotation.walkthrough: "Not all there is" reads as one phrase; the definition stops at "there", and the anagram begins with "is".
annotation.definitionFit: Someone scatterbrained is disorganised and forgetful, not all there.

clue.text: Old instrument accountant used in novel (7)

annotation.surface: An antique instrument has been hired by a finance professional for some purpose.
annotation.walkthrough: CA is a chartered accountant.
annotation.definitionFit: Rebecca is Daphne du Maurier's best-known novel.

clue.text: Law enforcers worried to act as go-between? (11)

blocks.note: as in something that ate at you, gnawed at you

annotation.surface: Police officers, anxious, are asked to mediate between two parties.
annotation.walkthrough: "Worried" looks like it should be an anagram of the police; it is ATE, as in worry eating at someone.
annotation.definitionFit: To interpolate is to insert something between other things, so it stands in the middle like a go-between.

clue.text: Small Frenchman gets up, leaving (6)

indicators.note: In a down clue, getting up means reading from bottom to top.

annotation.surface: A short Frenchman rises from his seat and walks out.
annotation.walkthrough: Crossword Frenchmen are often a common French name, here Serge.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: egress is the formal, often legal, word for a way out or the act of going out.

clue.text: Pupil after school time in a work station (8)

blocks.note: a learner, as on an L-plate

annotation.surface: A student stays behind after lessons, working at a desk.
annotation.walkthrough: "After" places the pupil last even though it comes first in the clue; a learner driver displays an L-plate.
annotation.definitionFit: A terminal is a computer station where someone does their work.

clue.text: Queen's mate closed motorway (3)

blocks.note: as in a door pulled to
British motorways are numbered M1, M25 and so on

annotation.surface: The consort of a queen is held up because the motorway is shut.
annotation.walkthrough: A queen is also a female cat; her mate is a tom. TO means closed, as when a door is pushed to.
annotation.definitionFit: A tom is a male cat, the natural partner of a queen, which is a female cat.

clue.text: Instrument in Volvo car I navigated (7)

indicators.note: The answer sits inside the run of words that follows.

annotation.surface: Someone recalls a musical instrument lying in the Volvo they drove.
annotation.walkthrough: The answer spans four words, starting at the last letter of Volvo.
annotation.definitionFit: An ocarina is a small egg-shaped wind instrument.

clue.text: Gangster's weapon with last of ammunition in defeated warlord -- about time (4-3,7)

indicators.note: Take only the final letter of the next word.
The N goes inside the letters for defeated.
The letters for warlord go around T.

blocks.note: to see off is to defeat, so defeated is saw off

annotation.surface: A mobster's gun fires its final bullet into a beaten warlord, and not before time.
annotation.walkthrough: SAW OFF means defeated, as in seeing off a rival. A shogun was a Japanese military ruler.
annotation.definitionFit: A sawn-off shotgun, its barrel shortened for concealment, is the classic weapon of the armed robber.

clue.text: Source of authority -- a royal one with bite (7)

annotation.surface: An authority figure is described as a monarch with teeth.
annotation.walkthrough: R is the common abbreviation for royal.
annotation.definitionFit: An arbiter has the final say, the one whose judgement settles things.

clue.text: Spirited item at tea dance needs bachelor (3,4)

annotation.surface: A lively guest at a tea dance is in want of an unmarried partner.
annotation.walkthrough: "Spirited" suggests a lively person at the tea dance; it means soaked in spirit, and "tea dance" splits between the definition and the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: A rum baba is a small sponge cake soaked in rum syrup, a spirited item to serve at tea.

clue.text: Investigator doesn't finish college (3)

indicators.note: The word loses its final letter.

blocks.note: TECH, a technical college, without its last letter

annotation.surface: A detective drops out of college before completing the course.
annotation.walkthrough: TEC is short for detective; a tech is a technical college.
annotation.definitionFit: Tec is informal shorthand for a detective, an investigator.

clue.text: Cheers about one charged following provincial university's punishment (11)

indicators.note: Turn the word for cheers around.
The rest comes after the word for provincial.

blocks.note: as in live, a switched-on circuit

annotation.surface: Someone is thanked after being charged with an offence against a regional university.
annotation.walkthrough: TA is British slang for thank you. At Oxford and Cambridge, sending a student away from the university for a time is called rustication.
annotation.definitionFit: Rustication is the temporary suspension of a student, sent down to the country for a term.

clue.text: Lousy batsmen I see being out a lot (11)

indicators.note: Something lousy is poor and messed up, so the letters are jumbled.

annotation.surface: A cricket fan complains that the poor batsmen keep getting out.
annotation.walkthrough: The cricket picture makes "out" mean dismissed; in the definition it means away from work.
annotation.definitionFit: Absenteeism is habitual absence from work or school, being out a lot.

clue.text: Argue about a boy (6)

annotation.surface: Two people quarrel over a child.
annotation.walkthrough: RE is the Latin-derived "regarding", as in business letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the sense of making a case step by step, as in reasoning with someone.

clue.text: China to provide crew for old chopper (8)

blocks.note: china plate is rhyming slang for mate
to staff is to supply with workers

annotation.surface: The Chinese are asked to find a crew for an old helicopter.
annotation.walkthrough: "China" and "chopper" suggest a country and a helicopter. China is Cockney rhyming slang: china plate, mate. A chopper here is an axe.
annotation.definitionFit: A palstaff, or palstave, is a Bronze Age axe head, an ancient chopping tool.

clue.text: One may be Googling 'Brand, entertainer' (8)

blocks.note: to brand is to burn a mark, to sear

annotation.surface: Someone types the name of the comedian Russell Brand into a search engine.
annotation.walkthrough: The capital on Brand makes it look like the comedian Russell Brand; it is the verb, to mark by burning.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone Googling is searching the internet, a searcher.

clue.text: Sybil about to sing chorus knocking back traditional drinks (4,4)

indicators.note: The prophetess's letters go around the chorus.
The whole assembly is then turned round.

blocks.note: a sibyl was a prophetess; the container goes around the chorus
the meaningless refrain of a song

annotation.surface: A woman named Sybil is about to join in a song while downing old-fashioned drinks.
annotation.walkthrough: Sybil looks like a woman's name but stands for a sibyl, a prophetess, so SEER. "Knocking back" suggests drinking; it reverses the lot.
annotation.definitionFit: Real ales are traditional cask-conditioned British beers.

clue.text: Redcoat's dashing style (3,4)

annotation.surface: A British soldier in his red uniform cuts a stylish figure.
annotation.walkthrough: "'s" stands for is, joining wordplay to definition. A redcoat was a British soldier.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by category: the geometric decorative look of the 1920s and 30s is one particular style of design.

clue.text: Birds heading off for Scottish islands (6)

indicators.note: The word loses its first letter, its head.

annotation.surface: A flock of birds sets off towards islands off Scotland.
annotation.walkthrough: "Inch" is a Scottish word for a small island, as in Inchcolm.
annotation.definitionFit: In Scotland an inch is a small island, so inches are Scottish islands.

clue.text: Outside Scottish town is rustic farmyard feature (7)

indicators.note: The word for rustic goes around the town.

blocks.note: a country bumpkin; it goes around the town
the town on the Ayrshire coast

annotation.surface: A rural feature stands on the outskirts of a Scottish town.
annotation.walkthrough: Ayr is a town in south-west Scotland. The clue's order puts "Outside" first, but it acts on the town and the rustic.
annotation.definitionFit: A hayrick is a stack of hay, a familiar sight in a farmyard.

clue.text: Mischievous fellow and posh one make light conversation (6)

annotation.surface: A prankster and an upper-class type chat together.
annotation.walkthrough: A nob is British slang for a posh person; a hob is a household sprite, as in hobgoblin.
annotation.definitionFit: To hobnob is to mix and chat socially, especially with the well-connected.

clue.text: Fashionable hero vetoing changes (2,3,6)

annotation.surface: A stylish champion blocks proposed reforms.
annotation.walkthrough: "Changes" looks like the noun being vetoed; it is the verb that rearranges.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: this dated jazz-age slang for being with it, up to date, means fashionable.

clue.text: Sounds like greeting current in Somerset (3)

indicators.note: Say the greeting aloud to hear the answer.

annotation.surface: A hello that is currently popular in the West Country.
annotation.walkthrough: "Current" means a flow of water here: the Yeo is a river in Somerset, a county in south-west England.
annotation.definitionFit: The River Yeo flows through Somerset, so it is a current there.

clue.text: Fiddlesticks made of Oriental woods (7)

annotation.surface: Violin bows crafted from Eastern timbers.
annotation.walkthrough: Fiddlesticks look like violin bows made of wood; the word is an exclamation meaning nonsense.
annotation.definitionFit: Both are dismissive exclamations meaning rubbish, words you say when you don't believe a claim.

clue.text: Lapwing's regularly taken bit of cereal (3)

indicators.note: Letters taken at regular intervals means picking them at evenly spaced steps, here every second one.

blocks.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters of lapwing

annotation.surface: A lapwing, a bird, regularly pecks at grain.
annotation.walkthrough: Only the even letters of LAPWING are taken; the 's is part of the surface.
annotation.definitionFit: An awn is the bristle on an ear of barley or other cereal.

clue.text: Fixing pole, not very well (7)

annotation.surface: Someone repairing a post makes a poor job of it.
annotation.walkthrough: "Not very well" reads as a comment on the fixing; it is AILING.
annotation.definitionFit: Nailing something is fixing it in place with nails.

clue.text: Boorish type in noble line to do damage to family (7,7)

annotation.surface: An oafish member of an aristocratic lineage ruins his relatives.
annotation.walkthrough: RY stands for railway, a railway line.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the phrase names an awkward, unsophisticated rustic, the very picture of a boor.
